note:
Golden conformance vectors for the Catenary wire protocol (IDEA-27 / R4).

These are the actual anti-drift mechanism. Generating types from one schema makes the two clients agree about SHAPE; it does not make them agree about BEHAVIOUR — whether an absent optional is omitted or emitted as null, whether an unknown attachment kind drops the attachment or the whole message, whether a timestamp survives a decode/encode round trip unchanged. Every one of those is a place two hand-written implementations diverge, and none of them is a type error.

So: every runner (TypeScript, Dart, Go) reads THIS file, and each case must produce the same answer in every language.

Expectations:
  roundtrip — decode succeeds, and re-encoding yields `encoded` if present, otherwise `json` itself, compared as canonical JSON (keys sorted recursively, so key order is not asserted and everything else is).
  ignore    — decode returns the language's null/nil. Only meaningful for the union types, where an unrecognised tag must be skipped rather than raised.
  reject    — decode fails. The schema's constraints are only real if violating them is an error.
  tolerate  — the answer DIFFERS BY SIDE, and this is the only expectation that does (CANT-74). The two CLIENT runners (TypeScript, Dart) treat it exactly as `roundtrip` against `encoded`, where the unknown enum value has been replaced by the sentinel `unknown`; the SERVER runner (Go) treats it exactly as `reject`. Which side a runner is on is a fact about the runner, stated once in its header. Only enums a client can RECEIVE get this treatment; an enum only a client authors is closed everywhere and stays `reject`.

All three runners run all four kinds; nothing is skipped anywhere. The Go runner skipped `reject` until
CANT-25 gave the generated types an UnmarshalJSON that enforces the schema's constraints.

CREDENTIAL FIXTURES ARE DELIBERATELY LOW-ENTROPY AND SELF-DESCRIBING. A `Token` is 43 characters of base64url, which is exactly the shape a secret scanner is built to flag — and 32 random-looking bytes in a checked-in file trips one on every pull request that touches this file. An alarm that always fires is an alarm nobody reads. These strings satisfy the pattern, say what they are, and match nothing: the server stores hashes and looks them up, so a fixture token is not a credential anywhere.

cases.name: client_hello_full
cases.why: Every optional present. Resuming from a cursor is the normal case for a client that has been running.

cases.name: client_hello_fresh_device
cases.why: No optionals at all. A brand-new install has no cursor, and the absent field must be OMITTED on re-encode rather than emitted as null — the property that keeps `absent` and `null` from becoming two different states.

cases.name: ping_from_client
cases.why: R1's application-level heartbeat.

cases.name: ping_from_server
cases.why: The SAME frame decoded as a server frame. Ping and Pong belong to both unions, which in Dart means one class implementing two sealed types — the one structural thing a naive generator gets wrong by picking a single parent. If this case passes in Dart, the dual membership is real.

cases.name: pong_from_client
cases.why: Echoes the ping id verbatim; matching by id is what makes a missed pong countable.

cases.name: client_send_text
cases.why: The ordinary case. `client_id` is the idempotency key and is reused verbatim on every retry.

cases.name: client_send_voice_reply
cases.why: A voice note answering an earlier message. The client sends only an upload handle and a message id — never dimensions, peaks or a reply preview, all of which the server computes so the two clients cannot compute them differently.

cases.name: client_read
cases.why: Read receipts are a high-water mark, never per-message.

cases.name: server_ready_resumed
cases.why: The heartbeat interval is SERVER-DRIVEN. If this number lived in two clients it would be two numbers, and the Flutter one would be discovered wrong in the field rather than in CI.

cases.name: server_ready_cold
cases.why: resumed:false means the client must catch up over /sync before trusting anything it renders. A boolean false must survive the round trip and not be dropped as falsy — the classic omitempty bug.

cases.name: server_ready_with_wire_version
cases.why: CANT-74 Ruling 3. The server says which schema version it was generated from, so a client that logs an unknown enum value can say how far apart the two ends are. Optional and additive: a client generated before this field existed ignores it under the unknown-fields rule, and nothing changes behaviour on it.

cases.name: server_ack
cases.why: The other half of the send/ack pair, carrying both ordinals.

cases.name: server_ack_duplicate
cases.why: A retry of an already-accepted send replays the original ack. R1's zero-duplication criterion is only checkable because this is observable rather than invisibly correct.

cases.name: server_conversation_frame
cases.why: CANT-113. Introduces a conversation before its first message, wrapping the existing Conversation record with every optional field present.

cases.name: server_conversation_frame_new_direct
cases.why: CANT-113, absent optional. muted, first_unread_seq and retention_days are all legally absent on Conversation and stay so wrapped in the introduction.

cases.name: server_user_frame
cases.why: CANT-113. Introduces a user referenced by a conversation's first message, wrapping the existing User record with initials present.

cases.name: server_user_frame_no_initials
cases.why: CANT-113, absent optional. initials is User's only optional field; every earlier User vector carried one, so this is the first to omit it.

cases.name: server_message_text
cases.why: Steady state: the frame carries the WHOLE message, never a pointer the client must go and fetch.

cases.name: server_message_voice_transcript_ready
cases.why: The feature the whole project is worth building for. Peaks are a stored array and segments carry word offsets for search's JUMP TO.

transcript.text: picking up the trailer at eight, should be back before the rain

segments.text: picking up the trailer at eight,
should be back before the rain

cases.name: server_message_voice_transcript_pending
cases.why: The async Whisper job has not landed. eta_sec is the SERVER's estimate; a client must not invent one, which is why it is on the wire at all.

cases.name: server_message_image_with_reply
cases.why: Stored dimensions fix the row height before a byte of image arrives — the property the blurhash placeholder protects. The reply stub is rendered server-side from the live source.

reply_to.preview: picking up the trailer at eight, should be back…

cases.name: server_typing_three
cases.why: ORDER IS NORMATIVE. Spec card F names people in the order they started typing, so a client that sorted this list would render a different string from the same frame — divergence with no type error anywhere.

cases.name: server_typing_empty
cases.why: Nobody is typing. An empty array must survive as an empty array and not be dropped as falsy — otherwise the indicator never clears.

cases.name: server_error_rate_limited
cases.why: `retryable` is the server's judgement, not the client's guess, and client_id attributes it to one outbox entry rather than failing them all.

cases.name: server_error_not_a_member
cases.why: retryable:false. A client that retried this forever would look exactly like a client with no error handling.

json.message: you are not a member of that conversation

cases.name: server_resync_required
cases.why: Named explicitly rather than inferred from a short stream: silent partial resume is how a client ends up confidently missing messages.

cases.name: sync_response
cases.why: The reconnect path. `log_seq` is the caller's new high-water mark, not the server's head — deriving it client-side by maxing over `messages` is wrong the moment a page contains no visible messages. `users` is what makes author_id resolvable to a name at all.

cases.name: sync_response_empty_page
cases.why: Fully caught up. Empty arrays and has_more:false must all survive.

cases.name: conversation_fully_read_with_retention
cases.why: ABSENT first_unread_seq means fully read. There is deliberately no stored unread count anywhere on the wire.

cases.name: conversation_freshly_found_or_created
cases.why: CANT-75. head_seq: 0 is legal here and nowhere on Message.seq — a direct conversation find-or-create just created holds no messages yet, and 0 is the honest answer for what a resync would count towards. head_seq is an inline 0..2^53-1 integer rather than Seq for exactly this reason: Seq's own minimum of 1 stays true for a message's ordinal, which is never 0.

cases.name: reject_conversation_negative_head_seq
cases.why: 0 is legal (conversation_freshly_found_or_created); -1 is not. The lower bound is real rather than merely inherited from Seq's own.

cases.name: message_at_max_safe_seq
cases.why: Exactly 2^53-1, the largest integer JavaScript represents exactly. The boundary must be accepted so the bound is a real limit rather than an off-by-one.

cases.name: message_tombstone
cases.why: A deleted message keeps its seq. Renumbering a conversation would break every other client's unread arithmetic.

cases.name: unknown_server_frame_type
cases.why: A frame type this client was not generated with. Ignoring it is what lets the server ship a new frame before every client understands it; raising would make every protocol addition a flag-day.

cases.name: unknown_attachment_kind_is_dropped
cases.why: An unrecognised attachment drops the ATTACHMENT, not the message. A client that hard-errored here could never be shipped ahead of a server that adds a type — and losing the whole message over an unknown thumbnail is the worse of the two failures. `encoded` states the expected result explicitly.

cases.name: unknown_field_is_ignored
cases.why: Forward compatibility in the other direction: a field this client does not know is dropped, not raised. `encoded` shows it does not survive — which is correct and worth stating, because a client that echoed unknown fields back would look like it supported them.

cases.name: reject_missing_required_seq
cases.why: A message without a seq cannot be ordered, and silently defaulting it to 0 would place it before every real message.

cases.name: reject_seq_beyond_safe_integer
cases.why: 2^53. Dart and Go would carry it exactly and JavaScript would not, so the two clients would disagree about ordering with no error anywhere. Rejecting is the only way the bound means something.

cases.name: reject_seq_zero
cases.why: seq starts at 1. Zero is what an uninitialised field looks like.

cases.name: reject_timestamp_without_millis
cases.why: Valid RFC 3339, and rejected anyway. Both forms parse everywhere and then sort differently as strings, which is exactly the kind of near-miss that survives review.

cases.name: reject_timestamp_with_offset
cases.why: A non-UTC offset. Also valid RFC 3339, also breaks string ordering.

cases.name: reject_uppercase_uuid
cases.why: Idempotency keys are compared as strings. An uppercase key would defeat deduplication and send the message twice — the exact failure the key exists to prevent.

cases.name: tolerate_unknown_delivery_state
cases.why: CANT-74. A client generated from this schema receives a `state` a newer server added. An enum a client can RECEIVE is open on the clients: TypeScript and Dart decode the value to the sentinel `unknown`, log the raw string once, and re-encode `unknown` — and closed on the server, which refuses it. Was `reject_unknown_delivery_state`; `sending`, `queued` and `failed` stay inexpressible on the server for the reason that vector gave, and this one still proves the server refuses any value it does not define. A client renders `unknown` as `sent`, the weakest state the server knows.

cases.name: tolerate_unknown_error_code_keeps_retryable
cases.why: `retryable`, `retry_after_sec`, `message` and `client_id` are honoured exactly as sent when `code` is one this client does not know. The client treats an unknown code as `internal` for rendering and never invents a retry policy of its own — the sentinel disturbs nothing beside it.

cases.name: tolerate_unknown_resync_reason
cases.why: The reason only changes copy; the resync happens regardless, so a client treats an unknown one as `cursor_too_old`. `reason` is a named `$defs` enum (`ResyncReason`) precisely so Dart carries the same sentinel as TypeScript here — left inline it would be a `String` in one client and a literal union in the other, and this vector would have two answers.

cases.name: tolerate_unknown_conversation_kind
cases.why: A REST-only type. `Conversation` is served only on `/sync`, where one unknown value would otherwise fail the WHOLE page and leave the client unable to advance its cursor past it. The policy reaches the REST surface by this vector rather than by a sentence; a client renders an unknown kind as `group`.

cases.name: tolerate_unknown_transcript_state
cases.why: Rendered as `pending` with no progress affordance: the transcript is not usable, and it is not asserted failed. `eta_sec` survives beside the sentinel.

cases.name: tolerate_unknown_reply_ref_kind
cases.why: Rendered as `text`: the preview line shows, and no play or thumbnail affordance is offered for a source type this client cannot name.

cases.name: reject_unknown_typing_state
cases.why: `TypingState` is reachable only from `ClientFrame`, so it is CLOSED EVERYWHERE: a client authors it and never has to decode a value newer than itself, and keeping it closed is what stops a client from authoring `unknown` into an outbound frame. All three runners refuse — the two clients included, which is what this vector pins.

cases.name: reject_unknown_outbound_attachment_kind
cases.why: The one inline enum left in the schema, on a client-authored type. Closed everywhere for the same reason as `TypingState`; a named enum on a server-emitted type is the only shape the generator accepts for anything a client can receive.

cases.name: reject_ping_without_id
cases.why: An unmatched ping cannot be counted as missed, which is the whole basis of R1's sever-and-reconnect rule.

cases.name: reject_typing_user_ids_not_array
cases.why: A single id where a list belongs. JavaScript would happily iterate the string's characters.

cases.name: reject_seq_as_string
cases.why: A numeric string. Go would refuse it, and a hand-written JavaScript client would very likely coerce it and carry on.

cases.name: enroll_request
cases.why: The only unauthenticated request this protocol has. Both fields required, so there is no optional to omit — the case exists to pin the token encoding and the device name surviving a round trip unchanged.

cases.name: enroll_response
cases.why: The whole bootstrap in one body: who you are, what this install is called on the wire, and both credentials with both expiries. Every field is required, because a client that received five of the six would be stuck in a way it could not report.

cases.name: refresh_request
cases.why: One field, and the device is identified BY it rather than alongside it. A request naming its own device id could disagree with the credential that proves it.

cases.name: refresh_response
cases.why: The rotated pair. The refresh token here is NOT the one in refresh_request — that is the whole property, and a client that re-sent the old string would be refused on its next call.

cases.name: reject_token_with_padding
cases.why: base64 standard encoding of the same 32 bytes: 44 characters ending in `=`. `=` is not a legal RFC 7230 token character, so a padded credential cannot ride `Sec-WebSocket-Protocol` — and an intermediary is entitled to mangle it rather than refuse it, which is the failure that would be debugged from a browser console. One identifier apart from the right answer in every language, so it is pinned here.

cases.name: reject_token_with_std_alphabet
cases.why: base64 raw standard encoding: the right LENGTH and the wrong alphabet. This fixture carries `+` and no `/` on purpose, because `+` is the subtle half — it IS a legal RFC 7230 token character, so a check written as "must be a valid subprotocol name" passes this while the encoding is still wrong, and a check written as "reject the base64 specials" is simply wrong about it. A `/` would be caught by either. The constraint is the base64url alphabet itself, which is narrower than the grammar and is what all three decoders enforce.

cases.name: reject_enroll_response_without_refresh_token
cases.why: An enrollment that hands back an access token and no refresh token leaves the device working for fifteen minutes and then permanently stuck, with nothing in the protocol able to say so. A missing required field must be a decode failure and not a null.

cases.name: message_send_request
cases.why: CANT-75's REST send: the same fields ClientSend carries below `type` and `conversation_id`, which this body deliberately omits — the path supplies the conversation, so there is nothing for a body value to disagree with.

cases.name: message_send_request_minimal
cases.why: Only client_id is required. text, attachments and reply_to_message_id are all absent — the same legal empty send store.NewMessage documents, reached over REST rather than the socket.

cases.name: reject_message_send_request_without_client_id
cases.why: client_id is the idempotency key and REQUIRED — a caller that omitted it would forfeit deduplication silently, and a bot needs the key more than a phone does because it retries mechanically.

cases.name: direct_conversation_request
cases.why: Find-or-create by handle. One field: the target's handle, never a conversation id, because the caller may not have one yet.

cases.name: reject_direct_conversation_request_empty_handle
cases.why: An empty handle cannot resolve to a user, and minLength: 1 refuses it as a decode failure rather than as a lookup that always misses.

cases.name: reject_heartbeat_interval_zero
cases.why: CANT-106. `heartbeat_interval_sec` is server-driven precisely so the 30-45s window under Cloudflare's ~100s idle timeout lives in one place; a property-level `minimum`/`maximum` used to be checked by nobody in any of the three languages, and 0 decoded fine — a client would ping in a hot loop rather than on the announced interval.

cases.name: reject_heartbeat_interval_too_high
cases.why: CANT-106's other edge: 91 clears Cloudflare's ~100s idle timeout with no margin left for a slow round trip. The same gap that let 0 through let this through too, since neither bound was checked on a property.

cases.name: server_ready_heartbeat_min_boundary
cases.why: CANT-106. The lower bound itself must still decode — a fix for `reject_heartbeat_interval_zero` that refused 5 as well would be an off-by-one wearing a passing test.

cases.name: server_ready_heartbeat_max_boundary
cases.why: CANT-106, the upper edge of the same boundary check.

cases.name: reject_missed_pong_limit_zero
cases.why: CANT-106. `missed_pong_limit` has a `minimum` and no `maximum` — a different shape from `heartbeat_interval_sec`'s paired bound, worth its own vector. 0 means severing before a single ping goes unanswered, which is not what R1's `missed_pong_limit: 2` means by the word.

cases.name: reject_client_hello_wire_version_zero
cases.why: CANT-106. `ClientHello.wire_version` carries the same `minimum: 1` gap as `ServerReady.wire_version`, on the CLIENT-authored side of the frame union rather than the server-emitted side — proving the fix reaches both unions' object decoders, not just `ServerFrame`'s. Zero is what an uninitialised field looks like, the same reasoning `reject_seq_zero` already applies to `seq`.

cases.name: reject_user_initials_too_long
cases.why: CANT-106. `initials` is two letters for the avatar tile and carries both `minLength` and `maxLength` — neither was enforced anywhere before this fix. Three characters is not a near miss the tile silently truncates; it is a value the schema already said was invalid.

cases.name: reject_ping_id_empty
cases.why: CANT-106. `Ping.id` carries `minLength: 1` so a missed pong can be matched by id — matching by arrival order cannot tell a lost pong from a slow one. An empty id used to decode fine, defeating exactly the matching this field exists for.

cases.name: reject_voice_attachment_peak_out_of_range
cases.why: CANT-106's nested-array case: `peaks` items carry `minimum: 0, maximum: 100`, a constraint on the ARRAY ITEM rather than the property itself, one level deeper than every other vector this ticket adds. A bar above 100 is not merely off the canvas's own 0-100 scale; before this fix nothing checked it.

cases.name: reject_conversation_retention_days_zero
cases.why: CANT-106, on an OPTIONAL property: `retention_days` carries `minimum: 1` because absent means inherit-global-infinite, NOT zero days — CLAUDE.md is explicit that code reading it as 0 deletes everything. This proves an out-of-bounds value is refused when present, not merely skipped because the field is optional.

cases.name: user_initials_cjk
cases.why: CANT-106 review. `minLength`/`maxLength` count UNICODE CODE POINTS; `.length` in TypeScript and Dart counts UTF-16 code units and `len()` in Go counts bytes, and the three agree with each other and with the schema only for ASCII. `internal/wireview/sync.go`'s `initials()` derives exactly this two-code-point value from "陳 大文" per its own documented test case — `len("陳大")` is 6 bytes, which a byte-counting Go check would have refused while both code-unit-counting clients accepted the identical page.

cases.name: user_initials_astral
cases.why: CANT-106 review, the surrogate-pair case: U+1D400 MATHEMATICAL BOLD CAPITAL A is ONE code point and TWO UTF-16 code units, so "𝐀L" is 2 code points (valid) but 3 code units — a naive `.length` fix in TypeScript or Dart would refuse this exact value while a byte-counting Go fix would refuse it for yet another count (5 bytes). All three must agree it is exactly 2.

cases.name: device_list_response
cases.why: CANT-117. Both shapes of a device in one page: a live one with `revoked_at` ABSENT, and a revoked one carrying the moment. Absent-means-live is the whole encoding — a decoder that emitted null for the live device would make `absent` and `null` two states, which the conventions forbid — and revoked rows are IN the list because a device row is never deleted and the column exists so that "was this ever revoked, and when?" survives.

cases.name: device_list_response_empty
cases.why: A bot has no device and never enrolls one, so this is its ordinary answer rather than a refusal. It also pins the empty array: `devices` is required, so an empty page must encode as `[]` and never as null or absent — the same property an empty SyncResponse page has to hold, and the one a `nil` slice in Go silently breaks.

cases.name: reject_device_without_created_at
cases.why: `created_at` is required and is the only ordering the list has. A device that omitted it would sort arbitrarily in one client and not another, which is exactly the two-implementation divergence the vectors exist to catch — so every decoder must refuse the page rather than render a device with no date.
